headings.title: Introduction to Positron Emission Tomography (PET)
headings.content: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is an advanced functional imaging modality widely utilized in modern diagnostic medicine, oncology, cardiology, and neurology. Unlike conventional structural imaging techniques such as standard X-rays, computed tomography (CT) scans, or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that primarily highlight anatomical structures, a PET scan evaluates metabolic and biochemical processes within the living body. In nursing practice, understanding the basis of PET imaging is essential for guiding patients and collaborating effectively with multidisciplinary healthcare teams. The technique works by detecting pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron-emitting radionuclide, commonly known as a radiotracer, which has been introduced into the body. As tissues with higher metabolic rates—such as rapidly dividing cancer cells or active areas of the brain—absorb larger quantities of the radiotracer, they appear as bright spots on the resulting computer-generated images. This high sensitivity allows healthcare providers to detect cellular changes and metabolic abnormalities long before structural damage or anatomical alterations become visible on a standard CT or MRI scan. For nursing students preparing for clinical practice and board examinations in Nigeria, recognizing the shift from anatomical to functional imaging is crucial. PET scans are frequently combined with CT scans (PET-CT) to provide both precise anatomical localization and functional data in a single imaging session, optimizing diagnostic accuracy and patient management outcomes across various healthcare settings.

headings.title: Underlying Principles and Radiopharmaceuticals
headings.content: The underlying principle of Positron Emission Tomography relies on the administration of radiopharmaceuticals, which are biologically active molecules tagged with a positron-emitting radioisotope. The most frequently used radiopharmaceutical in clinical PET imaging is Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), a glucose analog. Because normal cells and particularly pathological tissues, such as malignant tumors and inflamed areas, have an increased demand for energy, they take up FDG at a much higher rate than surrounding healthy tissue. Once inside the cell, FDG is phosphorylated by hexokinase into FDG-6-phosphate, but it cannot proceed further down the glycolysis pathway. Consequently, it becomes trapped inside the cell, a phenomenon known as metabolic trapping, allowing the PET scanner to detect the concentration of the tracer. When a positron emitted by the decaying 18F nucleus travels a short distance and collides with an electron, an annihilation event occurs. This collision produces two high-energy photons traveling in approximately opposite directions, which are then detected by ring-shaped detectors surrounding the patient. Other radiopharmaceuticals may be used depending on the specific diagnostic goal, such as ammonia labeled with Nitrogen-13 for cardiac perfusion studies. For nursing students, comprehending how these radiopharmaceuticals function highlights the importance of patient preparation, such as fasting, to ensure accurate metabolic tracking and prevent interference from competing endogenous glucose levels.

headings.title: Indications and Clinical Uses in Medical-Surgical Nursing
headings.content: In medical-surgical nursing, Positron Emission Tomography plays a vital role in the staging, treatment planning, and surveillance of numerous complex conditions. Oncology is the primary clinical arena for PET scans, where they are extensively used for detecting primary malignancies, determining the extent of metastasis, staging cancers such as lymphomas, lung cancer, and colorectal cancer, and evaluating the effectiveness of chemotherapy or radiation therapy. By showing whether a mass is metabolically active, PET helps differentiate between benign scar tissue and residual viable tumor tissue following treatment. Beyond oncology, PET is invaluable in neurology and cardiology. In neurology, it aids in mapping brain function, localizing epileptic seizure foci before neurosurgery, and differentiating types of dementia, including Alzheimer's disease versus frontotemporal dementia, by assessing regional cerebral glucose metabolism. In cardiology, PET scans evaluate myocardial viability in patients suffering from ischemic heart disease, determining whether hibernating heart muscle can be salvaged through revascularization procedures like coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) or percutaneous intervention. Medical-surgical nurses must understand these indications to educate patients effectively, interpret diagnostic orders accurately, anticipate specific nursing interventions based on the target organ system, and provide empathetic, comprehensive care throughout the patient's diagnostic journey.

headings.title: Pre-Procedure Patient Preparation and Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive pre-procedure preparation is critical for the success and accuracy of a PET scan, requiring rigorous nursing assessment and patient education. Since 18F-FDG is a glucose analog, elevated blood glucose levels can severely compete with the radiotracer, leading to false-negative results or poor image quality. Therefore, nurses must instruct patients to fast for at least 4 to 6 hours prior to the procedure, allowing only plain water. Patients with diabetes mellitus require special management and individualized protocols regarding their insulin or oral hypoglycemic medications to maintain stable blood glucose levels, usually tested using a point-of-care glucometer before radiotracer injection. Nurses should also advise patients to avoid strenuous physical exercise, caffeine, alcohol, and nicotine for at least 24 hours before the scan, as muscle activity and stimulants can alter glucose metabolism and uptake in the heart, skeletal muscles, or brain. Pregnancy screening is mandatory for female patients of childbearing age due to ionizing radiation risks to the fetus. Additionally, nurses should assess for claustrophobia, obtain a baseline set of vital signs, ensure informed consent is documented, and instruct the patient to empty their bladder immediately before the scan to minimize radiation exposure to the pelvic region and reduce motion artifacts caused by urinary discomfort.

headings.title: Intra-Procedure Care and Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content: Intra-procedure care begins with the administration of the radiopharmaceutical, typically via an intravenous (IV) injection. Once the radiotracer is injected, the nurse must ensure the patient rests quietly in a comfortable, dimly lit, and warm room for an uptake period lasting generally between 45 to 60 minutes. During this uptake phase, talking, reading, chewing, or moving should be strictly minimized, especially if brain, head, and neck, or cardiac imaging is ordered, as muscular activity can cause unwanted radiotracer uptake in specific muscle groups. Nurses should monitor the patient for any adverse reactions to the radiotracer, although allergic reactions are extremely rare. Prior to placing the patient on the imaging table, the nurse must instruct them to void one final time to empty the bladder. During the actual scanning process, which can take anywhere from 30 to 60 minutes depending on the protocols and the area of the body being scanned, the patient must lie completely still on a narrow sliding table that moves through the ring-shaped PET scanner. Nurses play a crucial role in providing emotional support, particularly for patients experiencing anxiety or mild claustrophobia within the enclosed scanner space. Clear communication, reassurance, and maintaining a calm demeanor help the patient remain still, ensuring high-quality images and preventing the need for costly and time-consuming repeat scans.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Care, Radiation Safety, and Monitoring
headings.content: Post-procedure care focuses on safe patient transition, radiation safety, and monitoring for any immediate post-imaging needs. Although the radioactive isotopes used in PET scans have very short half-lives (e.g., approximately 110 minutes for Fluorine-18), standard radiation safety principles—time, distance, and shielding—should be observed by healthcare personnel. Immediately following the scan, the nurse should assist the patient off the table, assess vital signs, and check the IV insertion site for any signs of infiltration or hematoma. A key post-procedure nursing intervention is encouraging high fluid intake, often prompting the patient to drink several glasses of water, unless clinically contraindicated. This promotes rapid renal clearance and excretion of the remaining unbound radiotracer from the bladder, minimizing overall radiation exposure to pelvic organs. Nurses should also instruct patients on proper post-scan hygiene, such as thorough handwashing and flushing the toilet twice after use. For a brief period following the procedure, usually the remainder of the day, patients should be advised to limit close, prolonged contact with vulnerable populations, such as pregnant women and infants, as a precautionary radiation safety measure. Providing clear verbal and written discharge instructions ensures the patient feels confident and safe when returning home.

headings.title: Interpreting PET Results and Complications Management
headings.content: Interpreting PET scan results requires a collaborative healthcare approach involving radiologists, nuclear medicine physicians, oncologists, and medical-surgical nurses. Results are typically reported using qualitative visual analysis and quantitative measures such as the Standardized Uptake Value (SUV), which calculates the concentration of radioactivity in a specific region relative to the whole-body distribution. An elevated SUV often indicates malignant, inflammatory, or hypermetabolic processes, whereas lower uptake signifies normal or hypometabolic tissue. However, nurses must understand that PET scans can produce false-positive results due to non-malignant conditions that also demonstrate high glucose metabolism, such as active inflammation, infection, granulomatous diseases (e.g., tuberculosis), or recent surgical healing. Conversely, false-negative results can occur with very small tumors, low-grade slow-growing malignancies, or when hyperglycemia competes with the tracer. When complications arise—such as extravasation of the radiotracer during injection, allergic reactions to adjunct contrast agents used in combined PET-CT scans, or acute anxiety and claustrophobia inside the scanner—nurses must respond promptly. Management includes applying warm or cold compresses for extravasation according to institutional protocol, administering prescribed emergency medications for allergic responses, and offering emotional reassurance. Documenting these responses and educating the patient on follow-up appointments completes the continuum of safe, effective nursing care.
